subject: let's migrate mc-stan.org to GitHub pages

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: let's migrate mc-stan.org to GitHub pages
parts:
Mitzi and I just sold our domain colloquial.com, and
I moved my own home page to GitHub pages.

There are two advantages:

1. As soon as something merges with master, it's live,
so no fiddling with upload scripts, etc. --- it just becomes
part of our regular workflow.

2. It's free.

The downside is that it's static pages only, but we're not
serving any dynamic content anyway (note to Andrew: if we want
CloudStan [aka "Stanbox"], we couldn't afford to do it on our
current host anyway).

All we need to do is add a repo named

stan-dev.github.io

and it'll be served as that page on the web.

On top of that, they let you link in custom domains for
free, so we'd be able to keep mc-stan.org. I'm less sure
about how to make mc-stan.com and mcstan.org redirect
properly.

I'm also planning to figure out how to use Jekyll, so if
we want to make the page look like every other open source
product in 2014 (rather than every open source project in
2004), that'd be how to do it.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: let's migrate mc-stan.org to GitHub pages
parts:
This sounds like a good idea. Would http://mc-stan.org simply redirect to the corresponding GitHub page? My only concern is that GitHub's https addresses make it more difficult to source .R files. For example, if we park Andrew's CRAN-incompatible stan() function in a stan.R file under http://mc-stan.org, then it can be sourced with the regular source() function that comes with R. If that file is under some https://github thing, then you have to do devtools::source_url(), which means the person has to have the devtools package installed. That is not too big a deal, but it is an additional hurdle.

Ben

to load in other packages? If so, we should add that to the
doc or have the function itself provide feedback (may be
automatic, so there may be nothing to do).

Andrew --- are you still getting crashes? If so, more
people using this function might help us figure out if
the saving/reconstituting models part of it is causing
issues. I've never had Stan crash either the terminal
or the GUI (though it used to hang the GUI when we tried
to do overwrites on the output, but that doesn't happen
any more).

I have to say, that beep is very satisfying.

Would it make sense for there to be the option of just a little bit of progress-report output so that the user knows when it’s half done, etc?  I’m torn on this:  the old rstan output was too much, and I prefer the current less-verbose option.  But for a long computation it’s frustrating to not have progress report.

One possibility would be to have a progress report after 5% of the warmup is done, then after 50% of the warmup, then after all the warmup.  Each time it could give a rough estimate of when it would be done.  (A rule of thumb could be that warmup takes 2/3 of the time, so we could take the time after 5% of warmup and multiply it by 30, then we could take the time after 50% of the warmup, then we could take the time after 100% of the warmup and multiply it by 1.5.  Maybe with a default setting that if the first time lag (after 5% of the warmup) is less than 1 second, it suppresses the output.

A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] let's migrate mc-stan.org to GitHub pages
parts:
On Thursday, February 26, 2015 at 10:44:46 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I have to say, that beep is very satisfying.

Would it make sense for there to be the option of just a little bit of progress-report output so that the user knows when it’s half done, etc?  I’m torn on this:  the old rstan output was too much, and I prefer the current less-verbose option.  But for a long computation it’s frustrating to not have progress report.

The parallel chains plus RStudio makes it such that I don't know how to do it. On Windows, the chains start in their own R process and nothing comes back to the main process until they are done. You can write to stdout or stderr but it doesn't flush to the main process until the end, so that is pointless for a progress report. On not Windows, you can see stdout in real time if you work in a terminal. But then you have all the chains writing to stdout simultaneously and it is a giant mess. I sometimes only output the progress of chain 1, but sometimes chain 1 finishes before the last chain even starts and it looks to the user like a freeze. Furthermore, it seems as if most people are using RStudio now and they don't direct stdout to the Console.

I think we would have to do something complicated like pass an R environment with an R progress bar to C++ and have the C++ update the progress bar.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] let's migrate mc-stan.org to GitHub pages
parts: On Thursday, February 26, 2015 at 10:44:46 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:

Would it make sense for there to be the option of just a little bit of progress-report output so that the user knows when it’s half done, etc?  I’m torn on this:  the old rstan output was too much, and I prefer the current less-verbose option.  But for a long computation it’s frustrating to not have progress report.

I put in a very hackish version that writes the progress to a file every 500 iterations and opens the file if you are in interactive mode. You have to refresh to see subsequent progress. It is annoying for programs that finish before you even have time to look at the file.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] let's migrate mc-stan.org to GitHub pages
parts:
It might be possible to spawn a separate process that reads the
progress and reports in some kind of standalone GUI. What
I'd really like is 4 parallel progress bar if we're running
four chains, each with an estimated time to finish that's
continually updated as (avg time per iteration * number of
iterations left). It'll usually overestimate remaining time
because warmup iterations take long, so maybe a rolling average
would be better.

Seems like a lot of work, though.

The right thing to do as Ben suggests is to run in threads where
we can easily control inter-thread communication within a single
process using semaphores and locks.

I don't think we should have something that requires user input to finish.

- Bob
